headline: BigGo Finance reports that investors this week sold off the bonds of CoreWeave, a US company that rents out AI data centres, pushing the yield on its 2032 notes to almost 15%, in what the Financial Times describes as a 'Darwin moment' for AI borrowers.
score_reason: Restored to the pool score of 7: the sell-off is confirmed by several outlets with figures (CoreWeave 2032 bonds below 80 cents on the dollar, yield about 14.8%, about $80 billion wiped off AI infrastructure stocks on 14 Oct).
importance_line: If lenders demand much higher rates from AI data centre builders, new building gets dearer and weaker borrowers may be shut out of the debt market, which hits the investors holding their bonds, though analysts expect a shake-out of the weaker borrowers rather than a wide default.
source: BigGo Finance, citing LSEG data and the Financial Times
summary: BigGo Finance reports, citing LSEG data, that the 2032 bonds of CoreWeave, which rents out data centres full of AI chips, fell below 80 cents on the dollar by 14 October, lifting their yield to about 14.8% against the 9.625% interest rate they carried when sold in June, and, citing the Financial Times, that the company's debts including leases reached $52 billion at the end of June. CoreWeave's shares fell 15% that day, with Oracle, Nebius and Dell also down, after a higher than expected US inflation figure of 3.7% for September raised bets on more rate rises; analysts cited by BigGo expect weaker borrowers to be pushed out of the debt market rather than a wide wave of defaults, and Startup Fortune adds that banks are still trying to sell the last of a record $38 billion data centre loan tied to Oracle.
notes: Read at BigGo Finance (two pages) and Startup Fortune. The Financial Times 'Darwin moment' wording comes from its headline only; the FT article text was not read. Figures differ slightly between outlets (14.5% to about 15% yield); BigGo's 14.8% (LSEG) is used.
